'''''Phyllophora crispa''''' is a medium-sized fleshy, marine [[red alga]]. This alga forms dense mats of up to 15 cm thickness, which influence environmental factors, thus creating habitat for several associated organisms.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Schmidt|first1=Neele|last2=El-Khaled|first2=Yusuf C.|last3=Roßbach|first3=Felix I.|last4=Wild|first4=Christian|date=2021|title=Fleshy Red Algae Mats Influence Their Environment in the Mediterranean Sea|journal=Front. Mar. Sci.|volume=8|article-number=721626|doi=10.3389/fmars.2021.721626|doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Description==
''Phyllophora crispa'' is a perennial seaweed growing up to {{cvt|15|cm}} long.<ref name="Bunker">Bunker, F.StP. D., Brodie, J.A., Maggs, C.A. and Bunker, A.R.2017. ''Seaweeds of Britain and Ireland Second Edition'' Wild Nature Press, Plymouth, UK{{ISBN|978-0-9955673-3-7}}</ref> It grows from a short terete stipe. The frond is firm bright red in colour and with flattened parallel sides. It branches dichotomously the tips being rounded. It is cartilaginous with the medulla, the internal parts composed of large compact cells enclosed in two to four layers of smaller cells.<ref name="Dixon">Dixon, P.S. and Irvine, L.M.1977. ''Seaweeds of the British Isles Volume 1 Rhodophyta.'' British Museum (Natural History){{ISBN|0-565-00781-5}}</ref>

==Reproduction==
The sexes are dioecious, that is to be found on separate plants.<ref name="Dixon"/> The reproductive outgrowths occur on the blade surface,<ref name="Bunker"/> and the cystocarps are on short stalks on the thallus surface.<ref>Newton, L. 1931 ''A Handbook of the British Seaweeds.'' British Museum, London</ref> The tetraspores are arranged in rows; on the surface of the stipe is special bladelets.<ref name="Bunker"/>

==Habitat==
Epilithic, found deep rock pools  in the lower littoral<ref name="Hardy">Hardy, F.G. and Guiry, M.D.2003.''A Check-list and Atlas of the Seaweeds of Britain and Ireland''.  The British Phycological Society{{ISBN|0-9527115-16}}</ref> and to a depth of 30 m in the sublittoral.<ref name="Dixon"/>

==Distribution==
Generally common around [[Ireland]], [[Great Britain]] as far north as [[Shetland]] and the [[Isle of Man]].<ref name="Hardy"/> Recorded also from Iceland, Norway, Portugal, Mediterranean and the Black Sea.<ref name="Dixon"/>
